Annals of Neurology

Accelerated Epigenetic Aging in Frontotemporal Dementia Highlights Smoking, Inflammation, and Metabolic Signals

Nijland D, van der Lee SJ, de Haan EM et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Case-control study with meta-analysis of two independent cohorts (peripheral blood DNA methylation)
Key Question: Is biological ageing, measured by the GrimAge2 epigenetic clock, accelerated in frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and what drives it?
Key Findings:
  • Pooled analysis (415 patients, 223 controls) showed greater GrimAge2 age acceleration in FTD (β = 1.17, 95% CI 0.46–1.88, p = 0.001), adjusted for sex, cell composition and smoking.
  • Component analyses showed higher smoking-related methylation, inflammatory markers (TIMP-1, CRP) and HbA1c in FTD.
  • Adjusting for smoking-related methylation attenuated the effect by ~48% (β = 0.62, 95% CI −0.01–1.24, p = 0.053).
Clinical Relevance: Suggests systemic inflammatory, metabolic and behavioural/lifestyle factors may contribute to FTD biology, though the findings are exploratory and not yet applicable to NHS clinical practice.
Limitations: Cross-sectional design cannot establish causality or direction, and smoking-related methylation may reflect disease-related behavioural change rather than pre-morbid exposure.

Annals of Neurology

A Recurrent 3'UTR Variant in CAPN3 Highlights the Diagnostic Impact of Non-Coding Variants in Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophies

Estévez-Arias B, Segarra-Casas A, Seoane P et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Case series with functional validation (clinical, histological, transcriptomic, and in vitro reporter assay data)
Key Question: Does the non-coding CAPN3 3'UTR variant c.*534T>C cause calpainopathy in individuals with persistent hyperCKemia and a single identified coding CAPN3 variant?
Key Findings:
  • 13 individuals from 11 unrelated families carried c.*534T>C in trans with a known heterozygous CAPN3 variant. Presentation was persistent hyperCKemia, commonly with proximal weakness and myalgia.
  • Muscle western blot showed absent or markedly reduced calpain-3, and RNAseq confirmed reduced CAPN3 transcript levels.
  • In silico analysis predicted a novel RBFOX1 binding site; luciferase assays supported a regulatory effect on expression (quantitative data not given in abstract).
Clinical Relevance: Patients with LGMD/hyperCKemia and only one identified CAPN3 variant may warrant 3'UTR analysis, which could resolve some UK "unsolved" cases currently left without a diagnosis.
Limitations: Small, selected cohort without a control comparison, and the abstract does not report whether the RBFOX1 mechanism was confirmed beyond reporter assays.

Annals of Neurology

Ambulatory Episodic Hypertension in Parkinson's Disease With Orthostatic Hypotension

Deraz HA, Dwivedi AK, Duque KR et al. · 2026 Oct 24
Study Type: Cross-sectional observational study (single-centre, consecutive patients, 24-hour home ambulatory BP monitoring)
Key Question: Are ambulatory hypertensive episodes associated with quality of life, orthostatic symptoms and motor severity in Parkinson's disease with neurogenic versus non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
Key Findings:
  • 59 patients (30 neurogenic OH, 29 non-neurogenic OH). In neurogenic OH, more hypertensive episodes were associated with better PDQ-39 SI, lower orthostatic symptom burden and lower motor impairment scores.
  • These associations were absent or reversed in non-neurogenic OH, and were stronger during daytime than night-time.
  • Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses. Abstract does not report effect sizes or confidence intervals.
Clinical Relevance: Daytime hypertensive episodes in neurogenic OH may partly reflect compensatory or treatment-related BP rises rather than purely harm, which could inform BP target-setting when treating OH in PD.
Limitations: Small sample and cross-sectional design preclude causal inference, and treatment effects (e.g. pressor agents) and reverse causation (better function enabling more activity-related BP rises) cannot be excluded.

Brain

Prematurity insults remodel cerebellar development and behaviour

Sanidas G, Simonti G, Ghaemmaghami J et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Preclinical experimental study (mouse model) with comparative human preterm cerebellar tissue analysis.
Key Question: How do maternal immune activation (MIA) and neonatal hypoxia, alone and in sequence, differentially remodel cerebellar development and behaviour?
Key Findings:
  • Hypoxia impaired granule cell maturation and excitatory afferents to Purkinje cells, producing impaired motor execution and stereotyped, sensory-disengaged social behaviour.
  • MIA expanded the granule cell progenitor layer and reduced Purkinje cell dendritic complexity, preserving social preference but altering the kinematics of social investigation.
  • MIA followed by hypoxia produced a distinct phenotype: granule cell proliferative arrest, progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and hyper-interactive social behaviour. Outcomes depended on insult identity and sequence.
Clinical Relevance: Findings suggest heterogeneous perinatal exposure histories may underlie variable motor and socio-cognitive outcomes in preterm survivors, potentially informing stratification and future neuroprotective strategies in UK neonatal follow-up.
Limitations: Mouse model findings with limited human tissue comparison; the abstract gives no effect sizes, sample sizes or statistics, and clinical translation is untested.

Brain

Serum β-synuclein predicts dementia conversion and mortality beyond amyloid-β and phospho-tau

Oberstein TJ, Schwarz J, Rudtke L et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Single-centre retrospective/longitudinal cohort study (memory clinic; n = 259).
Key Question: Does serum β-synuclein, a synaptic marker, predict dementia conversion, cognitive decline and mortality independently of CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 and pTau181 in non-demented memory clinic patients?
Key Findings:
  • Serum β-synuclein was raised in CSF-defined Alzheimer's disease (d = 0.69 vs controls) but not in A-T1+ "PASSED" individuals. Per SD increase: dementia conversion HR 1.40 (95% CI 1.11–1.77), mortality HR 1.33 (1.07–1.65), MMSE decline −0.20 points/year.
  • Adjusting for CSF biomarkers attenuated conversion and mortality associations by ≤13%. The cognitive decline association was largely attenuated by pTau181 (58.5%; P = 0.186).
  • Higher β-synuclein was associated with lower bilateral temporal lobe volumes (hippocampi, entorhinal cortex).
Clinical Relevance: Supports blood-based synaptic markers as prognostic adjuncts to core AD biomarkers, which may matter as UK blood biomarker pathways develop.
Limitations: Single-centre cohort without external validation, and findings varied with how pTau181 was normalised (Aβ40-normalised continuous vs staged).

Brain

Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface

Shen Q, Eliseyev A, Kansara V et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Prospective single-centre cohort study (n=41 clinically unresponsive patients; comparators: 22 conscious critically ill patients, 8 healthy volunteers).
Key Question: Can clinically unresponsive patients early after acute brain injury control an EEG-based, self-paced BCI, and does BCI control predict recovery?
Key Findings:
  • 13/41 (32%) unresponsive patients achieved BCI control (8/41, 20%, CMD-positive), versus 41% of conscious patients and 100% of healthy volunteers. Median signal delay was 49.8 s in unresponsive patients versus 17.1 s and 15.5 s respectively.
  • Recovery of consciousness by discharge: 31% with BCI control versus 4% without (OR 21.2; 95% CI 2.3–930.7). Functional independence (GOSE ≥4) at 12 months: 46% versus 7% (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8–81.6). No patient who was both BCI-negative and CMD-negative recovered.
  • All survey respondents (n=37) supported future BCI use.
Clinical Relevance: Findings suggest bedside EEG-based assessment could improve prognostication and detect covert consciousness, relevant to UK practice where withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment decisions rely largely on behavioural assessment.
Limitations: Small single-centre sample with very wide confidence intervals, and outcome analyses are unadjusted for confounders and potentially influenced by clinicians' treatment decisions.

Brain

TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy

Lastra Osua M, Perneel J, Vicente CT et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Narrative review (no systematic search methodology reported in the abstract).
Key Question: What is known about how TMEM106B genetic variation influences neurodegenerative disease risk, and can this be therapeutically targeted?
Key Findings:
  • TMEM106B risk and protective haplotypes modify susceptibility across FTLD-TDP, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and LATE, and contribute to healthy ageing and neuronal reserve; the causal functional variant remains unresolved.
  • Proposed mechanisms centre on variant effects on regulatory networks and protein levels, with emphasis on the aggregation-prone C-terminal fragment, endo-lysosomal function, proteolytic processing and fibril formation.
  • Therapeutic strategies under discussion include modulating expression, specific functional pathways and fibril formation. Current mouse and iPSC models have recognised gaps for studying function and cleavage.
Clinical Relevance: TMEM106B is a candidate shared disease-modifying target across TDP-43 and other proteinopathies, relevant to UK genetic FTD cohorts (e.g. GRN carriers) and future stratified trials.
Limitations: As a narrative review, it offers no new data, and the abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes or clinical-stage evidence for the proposed therapies.

Brain

Progenitor transcriptional alterations link fetal and adult pathology in Huntington's disease

Battistella M, Damaggio G, Conforti P et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Basic science / translational study: single-cell RNA sequencing of one human HD fetal brain and matched controls, supported by an HD mouse embryo allelic series and cross-comparison with published post-mortem and organoid datasets.
Key Question: Do cell type-specific transcriptional abnormalities arise in the developing HD brain and persist into adult pathology?
Key Findings:
  • Neural progenitors showed the most differentially expressed genes in the human fetal LGE and cortex, and were also affected in HD mouse embryos.
  • The progenitor signature comprised upregulated synaptic pathways and downregulated cell maintenance genes. It was moderately enriched in mouse LGE, and components persisted in adult post-mortem HD datasets.
  • Cellular interactions attenuated these alterations, suggesting a potentially rescuable signature. Effect sizes and statistics are not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: The findings support a neurodevelopmental contribution to HD and may inform the timing and targets of future disease-modifying strategies, with relevance for UK HD services and presymptomatic gene-carrier cohorts.
Limitations: The human fetal data derive from a single HD brain, severely limiting generalisability and statistical inference, particularly given variable CAG repeat length.
